title: Sharing and Grouping: Equal Shares and Equal Groups
seo_title: Foundation Sharing and Grouping Worksheets: Fair Shares and Equal Groups (Free, with Answers)
standard_text: Represent practical situations that involve equal sharing and grouping with physical and virtual materials and use counting or subitising strategies.
meta_desc: Free Foundation (Prep, Kindergarten) maths worksheets on sharing and grouping, matched to the Australian Curriculum (AC9MFN06): share equally, fair or not fair, make equal groups and count groups. 100 picture questions with answers.
key_big: Sharing equally means everyone gets the same.
key_sub: Deal things out one at a time. Equal groups all have the same number.
body_html:
Share equally

To share equally (fairly), give one to each person, again and again, until none are left. Everyone gets the same.

Fair or not fair?

If one group has more, the share is not fair.

Equal groups

Put things into groups of the same size. Count the groups, or count all the things.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do
Giving the total instead of each shareCount what one person gets
Counting the groups when the question asks how many in eachRead the question again: each or groups?
Calling a share fair when one group has moreCount each group and compare

faq.q: What do Foundation students learn about sharing and grouping?
faq.a: They act out equal sharing and grouping with real objects and use counting or subitising (AC9MFN06). This is the start of division and multiplication, without any signs.
Everyone gets the same amount. A good way is to deal the things out one at a time, like cards, until none are left.

faq.q: What if there is one left over?
faq.a: Then the things cannot be shared equally. Talking about the left-over one is a great early idea about remainders.

faq.q: How can I practise at home?
faq.a: Share snacks between family members, sort socks into pairs, or put toy cars into equal rows. Ask: Is it fair? How do you know?
